svg.text: Stool test vs colonoscopy: the honest tradeoffs
Two different ways to screen for colon cancer. Neither is wrong; they suit different situations.
Stool-based test (FIT/FOBT, stool DNA)
Colonoscopy
HOW INVASIVE
None. Done at home on a stool sample.
Yes. Sedation and a scope inserted into the colon.
HOW OFTEN
Usually every year, since it only checks for blood or DNA changes present that day.
Roughly every 10 years for an average-risk, normal result.
PREP NEEDED
Minimal. Collect a small sample and send it to a lab.
Full bowel prep the day before, plus time off work and a ride home.
SENSITIVITY
Good for cancer, weaker for small polyps, which can be missed.
The most sensitive option, since the colon is viewed directly.
IF SOMETHING IS FOUND
A positive result needs a follow-up colonoscopy to confirm and treat.
Polyps can usually be removed in the same procedure.
ACCESS
Wide. Needs only a lab, no specialist or facility booking.
Needs a gastroenterologist and an endoscopy facility, which limits access in many settings.
A positive stool test result should always be followed up with a colonoscopy, not repeated alone. Your doctor chooses the starting point.
